title: A class is a blueprint, and an object is the actual instance created from it.
when_to_show: When distinguishing between class definitions and object creation
body: A class can be thought of as a blueprint for creating values of the same type. Just because you define `class Dog:` doesn’t mean a dog is created right away. An actual object is created when you call the class name, such as `dog = Dog()`. When reading code, look at the class block to see what attributes and methods it defines, and then follow along to the line where the object is created to see where the actual value is generated. This card is not intended to help you memorize object-oriented concepts by rote, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are interconnected in actual Python code. When solving problems, check whether the class is a blueprint, when the actual object is created, whether `self` refers to the current object, and how dot notation is used to access attributes or methods. In particular, you should follow the execution flow to understand that `__init__` is a special method that initializes attributes when the object is created.
detail: A class is a blueprint for creating objects with the same structure, and an object is the actual instance created using that blueprint. Simply defining `class Dog:` does not immediately create an object; it is created when called, such as in `dog = Dog()`. When reading code, it is helpful to distinguish between the class definition, object creation, and attribute storage.

title: `self` refers to the current object itself
when_to_show: When you see code like `self.name` inside a method
body: `self` refers to the current object on which the method is being executed. When you read `dog.name` or call `dog.speak()`, you can think of `self` inside the `speak` method as referring to the `dog` object. Therefore, `self.name` is an expression that reads the `name` attribute of the current object. Rather than memorizing `self` as if it were a separate piece of information, it’s important to understand it in the context of which object’s method is being called. This card is not intended to make object-oriented programming difficult to memorize, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, check whether a `class` is a blueprint, when an actual object is created, whether `self` refers to the current object, and how dot notation is used to access attributes or methods. In particular, you should follow the execution flow to understand that `__init__` is a special method that initializes attributes when an object is first created.
detail: `self` refers to the object that is currently executing the method. When you call `dog.speak()`, you can think of `self` inside `speak` as the `dog` object. Therefore, `self.name` is an expression that reads the `name` attribute of the current object. You must understand the connection between which object called the method and what `self` refers to in order to interpret this correctly.

title: __init__ is executed the first time an object is created.
when_to_show: When looking at the __init__ method inside a class
body: __init__ is a special method that runs automatically when an object is created. It is typically used to set up the attributes the object should have initially, such as `self.name = name`. When you run `Dog('Momo')`, 'Momo' is passed to the `name` parameter of `__init__` and stored in the `self.name` attribute. When reading code, you should look at the object creation line and the connection to the `__init__` parameter together. This card is not intended to help you memorize object-oriented concepts, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, check whether the class is a blueprint, when the actual object is created, whether `self` refers to the current object, and how dot notation is used to access attributes or methods. In particular, you should follow the execution flow to understand that `__init__` is a special method that initializes attributes when the object is first created.
detail: __init__ is a special method that runs first when an object is created. It is typically used to set up the attributes the object should have, such as `self.name = name`. When `Dog('Momo')` is called, the argument is passed to the `__init__` method and stored as the value assigned to `self`. Let's look at the connection between the creation line and `__init__`.

title: An attribute is a label associated with an object.
when_to_show: When you see dot notation like `obj.name` or `obj.score`,
body: An attribute can be thought of as a label for a value held by an object. `student.name` is an expression that reads the `name` value held by the `student` object, and `student.score = 90` is an expression that creates or changes the `score` attribute. Unlike local variables inside a function, attributes remain attached to the object. When using dot notation, you must verify which attribute of which object you are reading or modifying. This card is not intended to help you memorize object-oriented concepts by rote, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are interconnected in actual Python code. When solving problems, check whether the class is a blueprint, when the actual object is created, whether `self` refers to the current object, and which attributes or methods are being used via dot notation. In particular, you should follow the execution flow to understand that `__init__` is a special method that initializes attributes when the object is first created.
detail: An attribute is a label for a value associated with an object. `student.name` reads the `name` value held by the `student` object, and `student.score = 90` creates or changes the `score` attribute. Unlike local variables inside a function, attributes remain associated with the object. Dot notation is used to specify which value of which object to read or modify.

title: A method is treated like a function attached to an object.
when_to_show: When you see code in the form of `obj.method()`
body: A method is a function defined within a class that operates on an object. Functions where the first parameter is `self`—such as `def speak(self):`—can be called by the object. When `dog.speak()` is executed, the `self` inside `speak` becomes `dog`. Methods can read or modify attributes and return calculation results. When reading code, first check which object `self` refers to within a method. This card is not intended to help you memorize object-oriented concepts by rote, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are interconnected in actual Python code. When solving problems, check whether a class is a blueprint, when actual objects are created, whether `self` refers to the current object, and how dot notation is used to access attributes or methods. In particular, you should follow the execution flow to understand that `__init__` is a special method that initializes attributes when an object is first created.
detail: A method can be thought of as a function defined within a class that operates in association with an object. When you call `dog.speak()`, the `self` inside the `speak` method refers to `dog`. A method can read or modify an object’s attributes and return the result of a calculation. When reading code, first check the relationship between the calling object and `self`.

title: Objects created from the same class each have their own attributes.
when_to_show: When creating multiple objects of the same class
body: You can create multiple objects of the same class, but each object can have its own attributes. If you create `a = User('A')` and `b = User('B')`, `a.name` could be `A` and `b.name` could be `B`. Even though they are created from the same blueprint, their actual values are managed separately. When reading code, you must not get confused about which object’s attribute is being printed. This card is not intended to help you memorize object-oriented concepts by rote, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are interconnected in actual Python code. When solving problems, check whether a `class` represents a blueprint, when an actual `object` is created, whether `self` refers to the current `object`, and which attributes or methods are being used via dot notation. In particular, you should follow the execution flow to understand that `__init__` is a special method that initializes attributes when an `object` is created.
detail: Objects created from the same class use the same blueprint but can have their own attribute values. If you create `a = User('A')` and `b = User('B')`, `a.name` and `b.name` may be different. When reading code, you must distinguish which object’s attributes are being printed or modified, and even if the names are similar, you should track their states separately.

title: A class variable is a shared value associated with the class.
when_to_show: When looking at variables assigned directly within a class
body: Values written outside a method within a class block can be considered class variables. They can be used as common settings shared by all objects. On the other hand, values associated with `self`, such as `self.name`, are instance attributes that each object possesses individually. At the beginner level, rather than trying to memorize class variables and self attributes in great depth, it’s important to practice distinguishing whether a value is associated with the class or with an object. This card is not intended to make object-oriented programming difficult to memorize, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are interconnected in actual Python code. When solving problems, check whether the class is a blueprint, when the actual object is created, whether `self` refers to the current object, and how to use attributes or methods with dot notation. In particular, you should follow the execution flow to understand that `__init__` is a special method that initializes attributes when an object is created.
detail: Class variables are shared values associated with the class, while values associated with `self` are typically instance attributes that each object holds individually. At the beginner level, it’s important to distinguish whether a value is written directly in the class block or stored in an object, such as `self.name`. Read the code while checking whether it represents a shared setting or individual state.

title: Object code is read in the order of creation, storage, and invocation.
when_to_show: When you need to quickly grasp the overall flow of a class's code
body: Object code is usually easiest to understand when read in the following order: class definition, object creation, attribute storage, and method invocation. First, look at the class block to see what values and behaviors it defines; next, check the object creation line to see if `__init__` is executed. Finally, follow the lines where attributes are accessed or methods are called using dot notation. Even in long code, following this order makes it hard to lose track of the flow. This card is not intended to help you memorize object-oriented concepts, but rather to serve as a supplementary guide for understanding how classes, objects, `self`, `__init__`, attributes, and methods are interconnected in actual Python code. When solving problems, check whether the class acts as a blueprint, when the actual object is created, whether `self` refers to the current object, and which attributes or methods are being used via dot notation. In particular, you should follow the execution flow to understand that `__init__` is a special method that initializes attributes when the object is first created.
detail: You can get a handle on the flow of object code by reading it in the following order: class definition, object creation, attribute storage, and method invocation. First, look at what values and behaviors the class promises, and check whether `__init__` is executed in the object creation line. Then, follow along to see which attributes are accessed or which methods are called using dot notation.
